content:
Hi all, we’ve just released AutoformBench: 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks from 24 advanced math sources.

Mathematicians formalized and audited the target statements. Agentic systems still have to build missing Lean definitions and supporting lemmas to complete the proofs while having access to the informal proof. We use Comparator for grading, with workspaces built using lean-eval. Thanks to everyone behind these tools!

For anyone interested in building agentic harnesses for autoformalization or theorem proving, the paper includes experiments, ablations and analyses of tool access, agent setups and cost efficiency.

The recent OpenAI/math release highlights how much formalization work remains. Across the nine models we tested, 59 tasks remained unsolved, and many successful runs still required substantial inference budgets. There’s still plenty to figure out.

Joint work with @Charles Arnal , @Vivien Cabannes, along with @Niket Patel , @Fabian Glöckle, @Bartosz Piotrowski , @Amaury Hayat , Julia Kempe, and Rémi Munos

Great work! I think we will need a lot more research in the coming months about what works and what doesn't work for autoformalization. This paper is totally in line with my intuition: Frontier models are perfectly capable of one-shotting sorry tasks without need for some over-engineered hardcoded system. If you think your custom harness is going to outperform the one builtin to frontier models... good luck.

However, one limitation of the study is that the size of the proofs studied here are relatively small and self-contained (~300 lines of code on average). One might think that for larger-scale proofs, some minimal amount of harness engineering may still be beneficial to help manage the complex web of dependencies, citations/references, and make sure that the output is in a format that can be useful to humans.

Thanks Jack! One clarification on LOC: ~300 is the median for accepted Astra solutions. The 59 tasks that no model solved aren’t included. I’d expect many of those to be on the higher end for the LOC.

I agree that larger more interconnected developments are an important next step. For multi-agent systems I see two relevant benefits: reducing the task time by parallelizing independent work and managing a model's context.
For the first benefit on the time scale, good orchestration by smart division of labor could certainly reduce elapsed time. But since our evaluation caps inference cost without imposing a time limit, we didn't measure that potential advantage.
For the second benefit for managing context our baseline harness supports long trajectories through persistent workspace files and conversation compaction. My guess is that persistent files and compaction may already provide much of the benefit at this scale of formalization (cf our other paper on simple harnesses ). DeepSeek for example solved 101 additional tasks after compacting its context window multiple times.

For much larger developments with complex dependencies and an emphasis on reusable output for sure is gonna require more complex multi-agent systems and extending the benchmark in that direction would be the natural next step.

Very interesting results! It seems that the models are tested with a common harness, which is also compared with Claude code on Opus 5. I wonder if other native harnesses could improve the results, especially deepseek harness. I've heard some good things about it. And it might even be easier to do the kind of engineering @Jack McCarthy mentioned on top of it due to its modular design.

Thanks Yidi! The design of the harness could indeed improve the results. Under a fixed token or dollar budget though I’d expect only modest gains from added complexity since more agents = more tokens. So the question is whether their division of labor improves progress per dollar not just progress.
The results here are for a capped budget of 200$ per task. I think that by just increasing the budget with the same common harness we can end up solving more problems with Astra, so more progress but that's not the main objective.
